title: The One Everyone Trusts
statement:
A team has n members labelled 1 to n. You get a list trust where each pair [a, b] means member a trusts member b. No pair appears twice and nobody trusts themselves.

The team has an anchor if exactly one member satisfies both rules:

  • the anchor trusts nobody;
  • every other member trusts the anchor.

Return the anchor's label, or -1 if no such member exists.

examples.why: Everyone else trusts 3, but 3 trusts 2, so 3 breaks the first rule.
1, 3 and 4 all trust 2, and 2 trusts nobody. The extra pair 1 → 3 does not matter.
A lone member trusts nobody and there is nobody else who must trust them.

constraints: trust[i] = [a, b], 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n, a ≠ b
hints: Think of each pair as an arrow from a to b. What does the anchor look like in terms of arrows in and out?
The anchor has n − 1 arrows coming in and 0 going out. You only need two counters per member.
Even one counter is enough: add 1 for each arrow in and subtract 1 for each arrow out. Only the anchor can reach exactly n − 1.

explain.intuition:
Draw each pair as an arrow a → b. The anchor is a member with n − 1 arrows pointing in (everyone else) and none pointing out. That is a pure counting question: no traversal needed.

Fold both counts into one score: in − out. A member can get at most n − 1 incoming arrows, so a score of n − 1 forces in = n − 1 and out = 0. Two members cannot both hit it, because the second would have to trust the first.
steps: Make an array score of size n + 1 filled with 0.
Scan members 1 to n; return the first whose score equals n − 1.
pitfalls: Checking only the incoming count. In the first example 3 is trusted by everyone else but also trusts someone.
Forgetting n = 1 with no pairs: the single member is the anchor, and the score test (0 = n − 1) handles it.
Using 0-based arrays and indexing score[n] out of range: labels run from 1 to n.

solutions.title: Check every candidate
solutions.idea: For each member, scan all pairs to see whether they trust anyone and how many trust them.

solutions.title: In minus out score
solutions.idea: One pass over the pairs builds in − out for every member. Only the anchor can score n − 1.

followups: You may ask only "does a trust b?" queries, with no list. Find the anchor in O(n) queries.
Pairs arrive as a stream and the list is too large to store. Does the score approach still work?
